title: Five Block inspector directions for SystemSketch
kicker: SystemSketch Block primitive · Babble & Prune · 31 Aug 2026
brief: Add one Block tool to the main toolbar. Choosing it immediately reveals Block settings on the right; after placement, the same surface edits the selected Block. Compare five genuinely different disclosure and layout models without changing the shared Block data model or tldraw interaction model.
defaultWhy: Inset Popout Inspector is the provisional default at 92/100. It makes the requested right-side inspector explicit without permanently narrowing the canvas, leaves visible whiteboard gutters around the surface, and gives Details and Connections room to grow. Its main cost is custom collision handling with the top and bottom utility chrome.
decisionHinge: The recommendation hinges on uninterrupted canvas versus maximum stock-tldraw layout fit. If 20 weight points move from Whiteboard flow to tldraw-native fit, Fixed Dock leads 93 to 84; otherwise Inset Popout Inspector wins because it keeps the board full-width and visually separates the inspector from application edges.
invariants: Exactly one Block tool appears in the existing bottom toolbar and uses B as its proposed shortcut.
Choosing Block or exactly selecting a Block reveals its inspector on the right.
The shared fixture is a 720 × 400 dotted board with the same decode Block, fields, ports, and toolbar state.
Details and Connections are views over one typed Block record; the UI does not create a second editing model.
Expanded remains a real frame-like shape with stock tldraw child containment semantics.
boundary: These are self-contained interaction sketches for human review, not production integration. The open/close and disclosure controls work in the gallery; document persistence, real editor selection, keyboard/focus behavior, responsive layout, port wiring, and accessibility QA are simulated. No Block product code has been changed.

requirements.name: Toolbar discoverability
requirements.why: The first success criterion is that a Block appears in the main toolbar and is easy to invoke.
requirements.passCondition: The selected Block tool is visible, named or unambiguous, and paired with a learnable shortcut.

anchors.1: Block is hidden or confused with another tool.
anchors.3: Block is visible but weakly labeled or spatially detached.
anchors.5: Block has a clear selected state, label, and B shortcut in the expected toolbar.

requirements.name: Inspector clarity
requirements.why: The second success criterion is immediate access to understandable Block settings on the right.
requirements.passCondition: A user can identify the current Block, its view, core fields, and the path to connections without hunting.

anchors.1: The editor surface is ambiguous or omits core context.
anchors.3: Core fields are present but hierarchy or mode is unclear.
anchors.5: Identity, view, fields, and Details/Connections structure are obvious at a glance.

requirements.name: Whiteboard flow
requirements.why: Blocks should enrich spatial thinking without turning the canvas into a form application.
requirements.passCondition: The canvas remains spacious and frequent Block creation/editing does not cause disruptive layout motion.

anchors.1: Inspector behavior repeatedly obscures or shifts the working area.
anchors.3: The workflow is usable but consumes notable space or adds a disclosure step.
anchors.5: Editing stays close to the sketch and the full canvas returns immediately when Block context ends.

requirements.name: tldraw-native fit
requirements.why: The port should follow supported tldraw tool, selection, component, and frame seams.
requirements.passCondition: The pattern can be driven by current tool/selection state and a supported right-side component without forking editor behavior.

anchors.1: Requires a parallel selection or canvas model.
anchors.3: Uses public seams but owns substantial coordination behavior.
anchors.5: Closely follows existing tldraw panel, tool, and selection conventions.

requirements.name: Inspector scalability
requirements.why: The surface must later hold views, ports, defaults, layout, and advanced settings without a redesign.
requirements.passCondition: Details, Connections, and later advanced sections have an evident information architecture.

anchors.1: Adding ports or advanced fields breaks the pattern.
anchors.3: The pattern can grow only through another disclosure layer.
anchors.5: Tabs or stable sections already provide a clear path for substantially more settings.

hardGates.name: One Block tool
hardGates.why: The toolbar must expose one coherent primitive rather than separate tools for each view.

hardGates.name: Selection-driven right inspector
hardGates.why: Block invocation and exact Block selection must reveal the requested right-side settings surface.

hardGates.name: One edit model
hardGates.why: Inline editing, inspector editing, and later menus must update the same typed shape props.

hardGates.name: Frame-native Expanded mode
hardGates.why: Expanded containment must use tldraw's real shape tree and frame semantics.

variants.name: Inset Popout Inspector
variants.thesis: Float a large rounded inspector card inside the canvas chrome, leaving visible gutters on every side while Block is active or selected.
variants.bestWhen: You want the clearest requested behavior and enough room for ports without permanently shrinking the whiteboard.
variants.losesWhen: The inspector must consume every available vertical pixel or custom collision handling with surrounding chrome is undesirable.

decisions.label: Disclosure
decisions.value: Details opens immediately; Connections is a peer tab inside the floating card rather than a buried accordion.

decisions.label: Canvas
decisions.value: The board stays full-width; the rounded card sits 16 px from the right and leaves separate top and bottom gutters for contextual and utility chrome.

decisions.label: Tool handoff
decisions.value: Choosing Block shows blank defaults; placement turns the same sheet into the selected Block inspector.

decisions.label: Implementation seam
decisions.value: Render a selection-driven component in front of the canvas and coordinate its inset bounds with the existing SystemSketch chrome.

proof: The same selected decode Block and toolbar appear in every preview.
Use the Hide/Show inspector control and switch Details/Connections to exercise the floating surface without changing the shared Block fixture.

fr1.evidence: The selected Block tool is labeled and includes the B shortcut in the shared bottom toolbar.

fr2.evidence: A large rounded card presents identity, view, core fields, and peer Details/Connections tabs while remaining visibly separate from the app edges.

fr3.evidence: The canvas does not reflow, visible gutters preserve spatial context, and the full board returns when Block context ends.

fr4.evidence: Selection-driven overlay state fits public component seams, but inset positioning and collision handling are owned SystemSketch chrome.

fr5.evidence: Two top-level tabs, scrolling, and stable sections can absorb ports, layout, and advanced fields.

g1.evidence: One selected Block item represents every view.

g2.evidence: A floating right-side card is visibly tied to the Block tool and selected Block.

g3.evidence: The preview exposes one field set; the proposal routes it through shared shape commands.

g4.evidence: Expanded is a view choice on the same Block, backed by frame-like shape behavior.

variants.name: Fixed Dock
variants.thesis: Reserve a stable right column whenever Block is active or selected, so the board and inspector never overlap.
variants.bestWhen: You expect long editing sessions, value stable geometry, and want the closest match to conventional tldraw side panels.
variants.losesWhen: Canvas width is scarce or frequently entering and leaving Block context makes the board resize feel distracting.

decisions.value: The complete form is visible without a popover or overlay layer.

decisions.label: Canvas
decisions.value: The working viewport contracts to reserve a 300 px inspector column.

decisions.label: Continuity
decisions.value: The selected Block remains entirely visible because the canvas lays out around the dock.

decisions.label: Implementation seam
decisions.value: Use the supported right-panel layout seam and derive visibility from tool/selection state.

proof: The board's right boundary visibly stops at the dock.

fr4.evidence: A reserved right panel most closely matches established editor layout conventions and supported component seams.

fr5.evidence: The dock has ample space and tabs, but permanent width pressure grows as inspector content expands.

g1.evidence: One Block tool owns all three views.

g2.evidence: The active/selected Block drives a visible right dock.

g3.evidence: Dock fields edit the same typed shape props as all other surfaces.

variants.name: Compact Peeker
variants.thesis: Show a small top-right card for the most common fields, with Connections and advanced settings disclosed only when requested.
variants.bestWhen: Most Blocks need only a title, type, description, and view while port editing is occasional.
variants.losesWhen: Connections and layout controls become everyday work or users need several sections visible at once.

decisions.label: Disclosure
decisions.value: Identity and core fields appear first; an expandable Connections section holds ports.

decisions.label: Canvas
decisions.value: A 230 px floating card leaves most of the right edge visible and never reflows the board.

decisions.label: Editing rhythm
decisions.value: The inspector behaves like a quick peeker, not a permanent application pane.

decisions.label: Implementation seam
decisions.value: Render a compact selection overlay whose expansion remains ephemeral UI state.

proof: The shared Block and toolbar remain visible around the smaller card.
Open the Connections disclosure to see the same packet and message ports.

fr1.evidence: The selected Block tool remains the strongest chrome element because the peeker is visually light.

fr2.evidence: Core fields are clear, but port context is one disclosure deeper than in the full inspectors.

fr3.evidence: The card does not reflow the board and occupies the least right-side area of the five directions.

fr4.evidence: A selection popover is a narrow supported overlay, though it is less conventional than a standard panel.

fr5.evidence: Growth is possible through accordions, but many port and layout controls would make the compact card deep and scroll-heavy.

g1.evidence: One Block tool is clearly selected.

g2.evidence: The compact inspector is anchored on the right and driven by Block context.

g3.evidence: Collapsed and expanded sections expose one prop model.

g4.evidence: The view switch keeps Expanded on the same frame-like Block.

variants.name: Canvas Quick Edit + Drawer
variants.thesis: Put frequent title/type/view edits beside the selected Block and reserve the right drawer for ports, layout, and advanced settings.
variants.bestWhen: Fast repeated edits matter and users are comfortable with a two-level power-user workflow.
variants.losesWhen: A single obvious inspector is more important than minimizing pointer travel or the split edit locus feels inconsistent.

decisions.label: Disclosure
decisions.value: A canvas popover owns quick fields; a named More button opens the deep right drawer.

decisions.label: Canvas
decisions.value: Common edits happen near the Block, while uncommon edits temporarily occupy the right side.

decisions.label: Editing rhythm
decisions.value: Pointer travel is minimized for rapid labeling and view changes.

decisions.label: Implementation seam
decisions.value: Both surfaces call the same Block command layer; UI state decides only which surface is open.

proof: The small editor sits beside the same selected Block while the deep inspector remains visibly available on the right.
Use the drawer's Details/Connections tabs to inspect the advanced path.

fr1.evidence: Block is clearly selected in the toolbar and the near-object editor reinforces the tool-to-object relationship.

fr2.evidence: Each surface is clear, but users must learn which fields live near the Block and which live in the drawer.

fr3.evidence: Frequent edits stay close to the object and the large drawer is needed only for deep work.

fr4.evidence: Both surfaces can use public seams, but coordinating their focus, dismissal, and shared state adds meaningful host behavior.

fr5.evidence: The full drawer can absorb all future sections while the quick editor remains intentionally small.

g1.evidence: A single Block tool still owns creation.

g2.evidence: The selected Block exposes both a quick surface and a right-side inspector path.

g3.evidence: The architecture explicitly routes both editors through identical Block commands.

g4.evidence: Expanded remains frame-native regardless of which surface changes the view.

variants.name: Inspector Rail
variants.thesis: Keep a thin right-edge rail for Block domains and open only the active section in a neighboring drawer.
variants.bestWhen: SystemSketch will soon add several inspector domains and users benefit from stable, compact section navigation.
variants.losesWhen: Only Details and Connections exist, making a permanent rail feel like architecture ahead of need.

decisions.label: Canvas

decisions.label: Navigation
decisions.value: Inspector domains remain spatially stable even as their internal forms grow.

decisions.label: Implementation seam
decisions.value: One host overlay manages the rail and section state while shape data remains in the tldraw store.

g1.evidence: One toolbar item still creates every Block view.

g2.evidence: Block context reveals a right-side rail and active inspector section.

g3.evidence: Rail navigation changes UI state only; all fields target one typed shape record.

checks: Exactly five structural directions, not cosmetic variations
Same board, selected decode Block, fields, ports, toolbar state, viewport, and fidelity class
Every preview supports a real disclosure or section-switch interaction
Five weighted criteria frozen before scoring; weights sum to 100%
Every score includes observable evidence and confidence
Four hard gates evaluated independently from weighted judgment
Pick, shortlist, reject, feedback, splice, copy, and download controls preserved
Production tldraw wiring, accessibility QA, responsiveness, persistence, and keyboard behavior are explicitly outside these prototypes
